To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the presence of a single betaA, gammaAAbu, Cap, or 4AMBx residue in a tetrapeptide can suppress the formation of specific b ions by inhibiting the intramolecular proton transfer step, and that the presence of these alternative amino acids in a peptide can influence the competition between b and y ions.

(1) the presence of beta-alanine, epsilon-aminohexanoic acid or 1,4-aminomethylenesulfonobenzene in a tetrapeptide influences the formation of specific b and y ions, and (2) the presence of gamma-aminobutanoic acid influences the formation of both b and y ions.

the presence of a betaA, gamma Abu, Cap or a 4AMBz residue at position 2 or 4 in protonated tetrapeptide ions can suppress the formation of b ions, and that this suppression is caused by the presence of a residue that can interfere with the intrapeptide proton transfer steps required for b ion formation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the influence of the presence of a single betaA, gamma-Abu, Cap, or 4AMBx residue on the CID of protonated tetraeptides.
the influence of alternative amino acid residues on the fragmentation behaviour of peptides.
the effects of the presence and positioning of a single betaA, gammaAAbu, Cap, 4AMBz residue on the tendency of a peptide to form b(n) and/or y(n) product ions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

beta-alanine, 4-amino-methylbenzoic, gamma-aminopentanoic and epsilon-aminocapronic acids do not influence the fragmentation of protonated tetra-peptides by inhibiting or blocking key steps in the fragmentation process.

the presence of a single betaA, gamma Abu, Cap or a 4AMBz residue can inhibit or suppress the formation of specific b ions, and the presence of a 4AMB residue can influence the competition between b and y ions by altering the relative proton affinity of the amide O atom.
the presence of betaA, gamma Abu, Cap or AMBz residues in a tetrapeptide does not significantly affect the CID fragmentation of the peptides.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the presence of a betaA, gammaAba, Cap or 3AMBz residue can influence the CID product ion profile by either inhibiting or suppressing specific intramolecular nucleophile attack or proton transfer steps.
the 'alternative amino acids' do influence the CID of tetrapeptides but the influence is subtle.

the 'alternative amino acids' betaA, gammaA, Cap and 4AMBz do not significantly inhibit or suppress either the intramolecular proton transfer or the nucleophilic intramolecular attack steps of the b- and y-ion formation mechanisms.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the CID of protonated tetrapetides containing beta-alanine (betaA), gamma-aminobutyratic acid (gammaAbu), epsilon-aminocaproic acid (Cap) or 4-AMinomethylbenzo acid (4AMBz) residues is not as straightforward as the CID of peptides with the canonical amino acid residues.
beta-alanine, 4-aminobenzoic acid, gamma-aminocaproate or gamma-aminobutyrates are not 'inert' in the gas phase.
CID of peptides containing alternative amino acid residues can be used as a tool to investigate proton migration pathways.
